description: Helicoverpa armigera, known as the cotton bollworm, is a highly polyphagous moth pest distributed across Africa, Europe, Asia, Australia, and South America. The larval stage feeds on leaves, buds, flowers, fruits, and seeds of many crops, causing severe economic losses. Adults are capable of long-distance migration, allowing rapid spread and multiple generations per year in warm climates.
symptoms: Larvae boring into fruits or pods
Damaged cotton bolls producing poor quality lint
Presence of frass and feeding tunnels in fruits or grains

life_cycle.eggs: Yellowish-white eggs laid on leaves, buds, flowers or fruits. Eggs hatch within 3–11 days.
life_cycle.larvae: Larvae feed for 19–36 days through several instars and cause the main plant damage.
life_cycle.pupae: Pupation occurs in the soil or plant debris; pupae overwinter in colder climates.
life_cycle.adults: Adults are light brown moths with a wingspan of about 3.5–4 cm and live about 10 days.
life_cycle.generations_per_year: Up to 11 generations per year in warm climates.

economic_significance: The pest causes severe yield losses in cotton, tomato, maize, chickpea and other crops. Larvae damage reproductive plant parts and reduce both yield and product quality. Secondary infections by fungi and bacteria may occur in damaged fruits.

monitoring: Regular scouting for eggs, larvae, and feeding damage
Use pheromone traps to monitor adult populations
Light traps can also help detect moth activity
cultural_control: Removal of crop residues and weeds
Deep ploughing after harvest to destroy pupae
Use of trap crops such as sunflower or marigold
mechanical_control: Handpicking and destroying larvae and eggs
Removal of infested fruits or plant parts

chemical_control.note: Chemical control should be used as part of Integrated Pest Management (IPM) and only when pest populations exceed economic thresholds.

genetic_control: Cultivation of Bt cotton expressing Bacillus thuringiensis toxins (Cry1Ab, Cry1Ac, Cry2Ab, Vip3A)
